strengths: Extensive empirical validation spanning model architectures (dense LLaMA, MoE Qwen2MoE), scales (66M–2B), datasets (C4, OpenWebText), and LR schedules (cosine, wsd), with consistent and reproducible gains for AdamWPower over well-tuned AdamW baselines.
Demonstrates scaling-law benefits (FLOP savings) rather than only fixed-scale improvements, which is more convincing evidence of practical utility at larger scales.
Shows compatibility/orthogonality with other state-of-the-art optimizer improvements (Muon, Blockwise LR), suggesting the method is a genuinely modular plug-in rather than a substitute.

Careful ablations: order of clipping vs. GradPower, robustness to (β1, β2) tuning, multi-seed variance analysis, downstream zero-shot benchmark evaluation, and wall-clock overhead measurement (~0.4%), which strengthen practical credibility.

Provides a plausible theoretical account (toy 1D model plus formal AdaGrad convergence theorems in low-/high-noise regimes) that qualitatively matches the empirically observed dependence of the optimal power p on batch size/noise level.
Transparent about the extremely close relationship to the pre-existing Powerball method, disclosed in an appendix, which is commendable scholarly honesty even though it affects perceived novelty.
The method truly is a one-line, hyperparameter-free (given single p) change to existing pipelines, which is appealing for practical adoption.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the sign-power gradient transform is essentially the pre-existing Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019), and the paper's own appendix acknowledges this was discovered only after completing the work; the main contribution is thus largely the empirical/theoretical extension to modern LLM optimizers rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Theoretical convergence guarantees are derived for AdaGrad, not for Adam/AdamW (the actual method evaluated at scale); the gap between the analyzed algorithm and the deployed algorithm (which includes momentum, bias correction, weight decay) leaves the formal link between theory and the main empirical method incomplete.

The illustrative case study (Example 5.1) relies on a highly simplified 1D uniform-noise, single-step-limit setting; while illustrative, its predictive power for high-dimensional, non-stationary LLM training dynamics is only qualitatively/anecdotally validated.

The power p is tuned on a single small-scale configuration (LLaMA 0.2B on C4) and then reused as p=1.2 across essentially all other settings; while the paper argues this generalizes well, the tuning protocol is thin and could risk being specific to the particular architecture/data regime tested, despite claims of robustness.

Explanations for some of the more striking empirical phenomena (e.g., improved training stability and outsized benefit for MoE models) remain speculative ('we hypothesize…leave to future work'), which weakens the mechanistic understanding of why the method is particularly effective in these settings.

Absolute loss improvements in many plots (e.g., Figure 3, Figure 4) are numerically small, and the paper does not report confidence intervals/statistical significance uniformly across all main results (only a subset in Appendix B.4), making it harder to fully assess whether gains are consistently significant versus run-to-run noise at larger scales.
Comparisons with other advanced optimizers/preconditioners (e.g., Shampoo, Sophia, Adam-mini) are absent; the compatibility study is limited to only Muon and Blockwise LR.

strengths: The empirical protocol is broad on paper: multiple architectures (dense LLaMA and Qwen2MoE), model scales (66M-2B), two datasets (C4, OpenWebText), two LR schedules (cos, wsd), and compatibility checks with Blockwise LR and Muon, which is a reasonable attempt at demonstrating generality.
The method itself is trivial to implement (one line of code, no new hyperparameters/optimizer state), which lowers the barrier for practical adoption if the effect is real.

Some care was taken with ablations: order of gradient clipping vs. GradPower, robustness to (β1, β2) re-tuning, and influence of batch size on the optimal power p, plus a multi-seed reproduction for two settings.

The paper attempts to connect empirical trends (optimal p decreasing with batch size) to a toy theoretical model and to convergence bounds for AdaGrad, giving at least a qualitative narrative for why the method might work.
weaknesses: Reported gains are numerically small in most settings (often ~0.01-0.03 absolute validation loss, and only marginal/mixed downstream accuracy changes, e.g., ARC-C actually decreases in Table 1), yet are presented as a strong, broadly applicable improvement; the practical significance of these gains relative to run-to-run variance is not convincingly established, since the vast majority of main results (Figs. 1, 3, 4, 5) are single runs without error bars or statistical tests — only two small-scale settings get a 6-seed check in the appendix, which is insufficient to support the sweeping claims made across dozens of other configurations.

The power p=1.2 is tuned on a single small-scale LLaMA/C4 configuration and then declared 'highly robust' and reused everywhere, but this is an assertion rather than a rigorously demonstrated property; given that Section 4.6 and Section 5.1 show the optimal p is sensitive to batch size/noise level, using a fixed p=1.2 across very different batch sizes, model scales, and architectures undercuts the 'robust transferability' narrative and raises the question of whether even larger (unreported) gains, or losses, exist for mismatched noise regimes not tested.

The core mechanism is confounded with the baseline tuning protocol: only the peak learning rate is swept for AdamW baselines (Appendix B.1), while AdamWPower reuses that same learning rate; because the power transform changes the effective magnitude/scale of the adaptive update (as shown explicitly in the theoretical section), it is unclear whether the gains reflect a genuinely new informative transformation versus an implicit re-tuning of effective step size/epsilon that a properly swept AdamW baseline (e.g. with different eps, or an additional small LR grid per model size) could partially or fully match.

The theoretical analysis is disconnected from the actual method evaluated: it analyzes AdaGrad (not Adam/AdamW, which is what all experiments use), under i.i.d. uniform or binary 1-D noise assumptions and a β2→1 limiting approximation, and under further restrictive assumptions (R<1 or R<1/4, specific noise-gradient alignment conditions) that are not verified to hold for real transformer gradients. The link between this toy analysis and the 'river/valley' or flat-direction story in Section 5.1 is explicitly acknowledged by the authors themselves to be only 'approximate,' weakening the claimed mechanistic explanation.

The qualitative claims about MoE-specific benefits (e.g., 'AdamWPower exhibits improved training stability, reducing loss spikes') and about the wsd schedule advantage growing over the stable phase are presented as explanatory findings but are explicitly labeled as unverified hypotheses by the authors ('We leave a detailed investigation...to future work'), yet they are advertised prominently in the abstract/intro as established gains of the method.

Comparison to the closely related Powerball method is relegated to an appendix added post-hoc ('After completing this work, we found...'), and the differentiation offered (scale/optimizer context) is somewhat incremental rather than a fundamentally new idea, which weakens the originality claim.

No systematic comparison against simpler/competitive alternatives that might achieve similar effects (e.g., tuning epsilon in AdamW, alternative learning-rate schedules, or existing sign/clipping-based nonlinearities beyond the single linear-transform strawman in Appendix C) is provided, making it hard to assess whether sign-power is uniquely effective versus other simple nonlinear or rescaling tricks.

Scaling-law claims ('potential for improved scalability,' 'gains may persist at larger model scales') are extrapolated from only 3-5 points per curve and are not statistically tested, so the scaling-law framing somewhat overstates the strength of evidence actually provided.

strengths: Extremely lightweight method (single-line code change, negligible 0.4% wall-clock overhead) with no modification to base optimizer hyperparameters, which is attractive for practical adoption.

Broad and systematic empirical validation: dense (LLaMA) and MoE (Qwen2MoE) architectures, model sizes from 66M to 2B parameters, two datasets (C4, OpenWebText), two LR schedules (cosine, wsd), and downstream zero-shot evaluation on six benchmarks.

Demonstrated compatibility/orthogonality with other state-of-the-art optimizers and techniques (Muon, Blockwise LR), with evidence that gains are roughly additive, suggesting the method is a genuinely complementary plug-in rather than a redundant trick.

The exponent p is tuned on only one small-scale setting yet transfers robustly across all other configurations, which is a meaningful and testable empirical claim, and the paper supports this with an extensive ablation on batch size/noise level that aligns with the theory.

Theoretical analysis is multi-pronged: an illustrative toy example matching the empirical p*-vs-noise trend, and formal convergence guarantees for AdagradPower in both low- and high-noise regimes, with proofs provided in the appendix.

Good scientific hygiene: multiple random seeds to assess variance (Appendix B.4), robustness check over a grid of (β1, β2) values, ordering of clipping vs. GradPower tested, and honest discussion of concurrent/prior related work (Powerball, Powerpropagation) with clear differentiation.
weaknesses: Theoretical convergence guarantees are derived for AdagradPower rather than for AdamWPower (the method actually used in the main experiments), leaving a gap between the formal theory and the empirical algorithm; the connection to Adam's momentum/bias-correction mechanics is not formally analyzed.

The 'flat/river direction' narrative used to motivate and interpret the method is heuristic and only loosely connected to the formal single-coordinate convergence proofs and the 1-D toy example; the claimed amplification of river directions is not directly verified empirically (e.g., via Hessian spectrum or noise-anisotropy measurements on real models).

Absolute terminal-loss improvements, while consistent, are often modest (e.g., ~0.015-0.045 nats), and the translation into 'equivalent FLOPs savings' reported in Figure 1 relies on scaling-law fits across a small number of points per curve; the methodology and uncertainty of this extrapolation are not detailed in the main text.

The exponent p is tuned on a single small LLaMA/C4 configuration; although transfer is empirically robust, there is limited exploration of whether a per-architecture or per-dataset tuned p could yield larger gains (the paper itself speculates an MoE-specific p could be better but does not test this), somewhat undercutting the completeness of the hyperparameter study.

Downstream zero-shot evaluation is conducted only for the largest LLaMA (2B) model, not across the full range of scales, limiting the evidence that pretraining loss gains translate into consistent downstream task improvements at smaller/larger scales.

Comparisons to other simple elementwise gradient transforms or sign-based methods (beyond a brief linear-transform argument) are limited, making it harder to contextualize how much of the benefit is specific to the sign-power nonlinearity versus other plausible nonlinear transformations.
